body.en: Relational tables are **structured**: every row has the same columns. JSON documents are **semi-structured**: each document carries its own shape, and two documents in the same collection can differ. Modern applications mix both — a product row with fixed columns (id, name, price) plus a JSON column for attributes that vary per product category. DP-800 tests exactly this mixed modeling.

JSON has objects (`{ "key": value }`), arrays (`[1, 2, 3]`), strings (double quotes only), numbers, booleans (`true`/`false`) and `null`. Keys are case-sensitive strings. No comments, no trailing commas, no single quotes. A **path** addresses a value: `$.customer.address.city` starts at the root `$` and walks down; `$.items[0].price` indexes into an array.

Historically JSON text was stored in `nvarchar(max)` and validated with `ISJSON()`. SQL Server 2025, Azure SQL Database and SQL database in Fabric add a native **json data type** that stores documents in an optimized binary format — smaller, faster to parse, and still presented to you as text. The dedicated JSON subtopic in Domain 1 covers the type, JSON indexes and when to choose each option.

- `JSON_VALUE(doc, '$.path')` extracts a **scalar** (string, number, bool).
- `JSON_QUERY(doc, '$.path')` extracts an **object or array** (keeps it as JSON).
- `OPENJSON(doc, '$.path')` turns JSON into **rows** — essential for joining JSON arrays against tables. With a `WITH` clause you project typed columns.
Mixing these up is a favorite exam trap: `JSON_VALUE` on an array returns `NULL` (in lax mode) rather than the array.

sections.code:
SELECT o.OrderId,
       JSON_VALUE(o.Doc, '$.customer.name') AS CustomerName,
       i.sku, i.qty, i.price
FROM dbo.Orders AS o
CROSS APPLY OPENJSON(o.Doc, '$.items')
     WITH (sku VARCHAR(10) '$.sku',
           qty INT          '$.qty',
           price DECIMAL(9,2) '$.price') AS i;

heading.en: Building JSON: JSON_OBJECT, JSON_ARRAY, FOR JSON

body.en: `JSON_OBJECT('key': value, …)` and `JSON_ARRAY(v1, v2, …)` construct JSON from relational values. Aggregates `JSON_ARRAYAGG(expr)` and `JSON_OBJECTAGG(k: v)` fold a whole group into one array/object. `FOR JSON PATH` turns an entire result set into a JSON document — the classic way to feed structured data to a language model or REST client, which returns in the RAG topics.

Paths default to **lax** mode: a missing property returns `NULL`. Prefix the path with `strict` (`'strict $.customer.vip'`) and a missing property raises an error instead. Use strict when silently missing data would corrupt results.

examTips.en: JSON_VALUE → scalars, JSON_QUERY → objects/arrays, OPENJSON → rows. Picking the wrong one returns NULL, not an error (lax mode).
The native json type (binary, optimized) is the modern default on SQL Server 2025 / Azure SQL / Fabric; nvarchar(max) + ISJSON() remains for older compatibility.
OPENJSON without WITH returns key/value/type triples; with WITH it returns typed columns.
Strict path mode ('strict $.a.b') errors on missing properties; lax (default) returns NULL.
